nicheStories.title: Trump's Lebanon fantasy is running smack into reality
nicheStories.description: On June 26, two official delegations — one from Israel and one from Lebanon — signed a framework agreement with great fanfare in Washington. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, openly enthusiastic, framed the event as paving the way toward “lasting peace and security” between Beirut and Tel Aviv.A month later, President Donald Trump received Lebanese President Joseph Aoun at the White House. Once again, Rubio welcomed the visit and reiterated the goal of disarming Hezbollah and achieving a complete and definitive peace between Lebanon and its southern neighbor.Like Tel Aviv, Rubio favors a top-down approach that centers on force and coercion. To neutralize both Tehran and Hezbollah, this camp hopes to combine strong military action against Iranian territory with maximum pressure on the government in Beirut. The goal is two-fold: to strong-arm the Lebanese government into sidelining Hezbollah and to permanently separate the Lebanese and Iranian equations.Within the Trump administration, not everyone is convinced that this roadmap is the most effective approach. Vice President JD Vance has for some time now made clear that he no longer believes that Washington’s interests and those of Tel Aviv are perfectly aligned, and he openly favors a de-escalation on the Iranian front. While Vance has not laid out a clear vision for his ideal end state, it would likely includean agreement with Tehran to keep its allied armed groups in the Middle East — Hezbollah foremost among them — in check. Incidentally, this would help stabilize oil prices and maritime traffic in the Gulf while preventing the war against Iran from becoming even more unpopular among American citizens ahead of the midterms. In this competitive landscape, the political and media buzz surrounding the Israeli-Lebanese issue offers an opportunity to bolster the supporters of Rubio and Israel at the expense of the vice president’s apparent preferences. All the same however, the Israeli-Lebanese process has very little chance of succeeding.In Lebanon, first of all, any agreement with Israel would face several legal and constitutional stumbling blocks. The consociational system, under which authority is largely divided up between the three main communities (Sunnis, Shia, Christians), leaves the president with little executive leeway. Since the 1990 signing of the Taif Accords, which marked the end of a 15-year-long civil war, the religious communities must adhere to a distribution of powers that determines the legality of political decisions. While Article 52 of the constitution authorizes the president to “negotiate and ratify treaties,” he may do so “only in agreement with the head of government,” and ratification will be validated “only after approval by the Council of Ministers.”The problem is that no government decision is constitutionally valid unless it is endorsed by all the major communities. Since the Shia parties expressed their opposition to the terms of the framework agreement from the outset, it is difficult to consider any future agreement viable.Similarly, any peace agreement with Israel will ultimately have to be ratified by the parliament. Given the body’s current make-up, the probability that the text will be approved by a majority of members is exactly zero.The Lebanese institutional framework is not the only problem. Trust in Israeli good faith is also a highly problematic issue. On November 27, 2024, Tel Aviv and Hezbollah signed a ceasefire. While Hezbollah adhered to it until March 2026 (that is, for nearly a year and a half), Tel Aviv never honored the deal: it violated the ceasefire agreement it signed in 2024 more than 12,000 times in less than a year. A new joke even emerged: “What does ‘ceasefire’ mean in Hebrew? ‘They cease, we fire.’”The systematic, large-scale destruction of the country’s south and the massive killings of civilians did not produce Israel’s desired results. Tel Aviv had ideally hoped for a polarization of Lebanese society that would lead to a civil war, in which Shiites would come under fire from their compatriots — or, at the very least, for a majority of Lebanese to condemn and permanently exclude Hezbollah from governance.The Israeli army’s brutal campaign had the opposite effect, adding fuel to Hezbollah’s fire rather than extinguishing it. In practice, the Israeli army has re-legitimized the Lebanese organization’s narrative that it has a special (if self-assigned) mission to defend the territory against the enemy to the south.This represents an extraordinary failure for the pro-Israel position on the issue. In January 2025, the U.S. and Saudi Arabia (alongside Israel behind the scenes) had pressured the Lebanese political parties to elect President Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, who were said to embody a “new era” for Lebanon. The new leadership promised, far and wide, that the United States was working to turn the Lebanese army into a military force capable of defending the country’s territory, which would render Hezbollah’s defensive rhetoric obsolete. They also tried to reassure skeptics by asserting that “diplomatic friendships” were enough to deter Israel’s potential trouble-making.A year and a half later, the Lebanese army not only still lacked the resources to carry out its mission but was openly fleeing, on orders from Aoun himself, in the face of the Israeli advance in the spring of 2026. Hezbollah, which Tel Aviv claimed to have decimated in the fall of 2024, was back in action as early as March of the same year. And there were no signs of any external “friend of the Lebanese government” to keep Israeli military force in check. The initial support of Salam, a Sunni, for direct talks with the Israelis in Washington quickly put him in an uncomfortable position within his own community. While Lebanese Sunnis may have internal disagreements with Shiite parties and, in particular, with Hezbollah, the majority of the community remains sympathetic to its pan-Arab, pro-Palestinian, and anti-Zionist heritage. This explained the stance of the Sunni elites, which, at first glance, seemed inconsistent but was in fact the work of a master of balance: as several MPs from the community explained to me in late March, they support the prime minister’s decision to send a delegation to Washington, but not the agreement that will result from it. Sure, there would be loyalty to the leader, but not necessarily to the outcome of his initiatives.Since the signing of the framework agreement, Salam has hence quietly distanced himself from the process and embarked on a tour focused on building closer ties with rising regional powers, led by Syria and Turkey. When asked about the status of the agreement, he tends to bristle and refer the questioner to the presidential palace.Worse, the head of the Lebanese army himself, General Rodolphe Haykal, was so openly critical that the American administration asked Aoun to let him go. And on signing day, the Lebanese military personnel who were part of the delegation refused to be in the commemorative picture. In other words, pressured by the U.S. and Israel to the point of defending options they themselves know to be unrealistic, the Lebanese authorities quickly found themselves losing legitimacy and credibility among their own people. Apart from the Christian far-right — namely the party of the Lebanese Forces, heir to the militia of the same name that embodied during the civil war years a brutal militia that collaborated with Israel — no Lebanese truly believes in what is being cooked up in Washington with the Israeli representatives. This helps explain why Hezbollah emerged from the 2025 municipal elections as the clear winner in every town and city where it fielded candidates. This reality check led Western governments to pressure Lebanese political parties into postponing the parliamentary elections scheduled for spring 2026 by two years. Little wonder, then, that even Rubio’s optimism has cooled somewhat. Commenting on Aoun’s recent visit, he merely cautioned that this was “only the beginning of the beginning.” One thing is certain: it was a rather isolated Lebanese president who took off from Beirut last week to accept Trump’s invitation. In most of the Lebanese capital’s political salons, regardless of sectarian affiliation, the prevailing sentiment is: “Good luck, my dear. It’ll all be over in November 2028!”

nicheStories.title: How much is your support for Israel worth? Try $1 billion.
nicheStories.description: Israel is spending wads of cash on public diplomacy in a desperate attempt to reverse waning American support for the country after it stands accused of genocide in Gaza and pushing the U.S. into the Iran war.Since Oct. 7, Israel has spent over a billion dollars on global “hasbara” — television appearances, social media campaigns, chat-bot training, and other efforts to influence how people think about Israel. And this “public diplomacy” budget more than quadrupled in the last year alone. To understand these efforts to win back American hearts and minds, we welcomed Quincy Institute Research Fellow Nick Cleveland-Stout to the latest episode of Always at War. Nick’s latest research is the most-definitive accounting yet of Israel's new approach to winning over American’s hearts and minds.Nick’s findings surface a surprising development in Israel’s influence efforts: while the country used to rely almost exclusively on wealthy, sympathetic advocates tilting the policy process toward Israel’s interest via American lobbying groups like AIPAC, Israel has recently been forced to hire U.S. contractors and firms that have to register as foreign agents under FARA. While the transition signals Israel's increasing desperation, it also allows us to see who Israel is hiring and for what. Take for example, Trump's former campaign manager Brad Parscale, who is currently the proud holder of three of Israel’s largest contracts. His main gig: running a mass texting campaign on behalf of Israel while posing as mysterious “peace” groups like “Allies for Peace.” Or, to take another example, the public diplomacy group Targeted Communications Global, which has spent nearly $10 million to run ads on places like X, the Daily Caller, and Breitbart. It turns out, Israel is more worried about maintaining their right-leaning supporters. But perhaps the most shocking revelation is just how much time and money Tel Aviv is spending on “training” our chat bots — think Claude, ChatGPT, or Grok. The Israeli government is actually paying for “LLM poisoning” — developing pro-Israel websites that feed information to these chatbots whenever they’re asked about Israel. The apparent goal is that, when you ask about a straightforward incident — like Hind Rajab’s murder by the IDF — the chatbot will feed you a “he-said, she-said” story that features Israel’s justifications for shooting a five-year old, not a straight, factual accounting of eventsBut the question remains, will the tens of millions Israel is spending on public diplomacy actually work? Will a sophisticated and expensive influence campaign really change Americans’ minds about Washington’s perpetual blank checks for Israel?Tune in and find out.

nicheStories.title: Houthis v. Saudi Arabia: Round 2. This time it's regional.
nicheStories.description: On July 28, Saudi air defenses shot down drones launched from Iraqi territory by “Iran-affiliated terrorist militias,” a Saudi ministry of defense statement read.The attacks targeted oil facilities in the Eastern Province and at the capital, Riyadh, itself. Days earlier, Houthi forces in Yemen said they had hit “sensitive” oil transport sites linking the Eastern Province to the Red Sea export hub of Yanbu. Satellite images showed smoke over the kingdom's most important oil infrastructure.Both attacks come amid a wider escalation that began with the Houthis’ declared naval blockade of Saudi ports, followed by strikes on several ships and an exchange of missile fire with the kingdom. The Houthis say they will lift the blockade only once Saudi Arabia ends what they call a “blockade” on Yemen; they also have separate financial demands, chiefly, a demand for public-sector salaries and a share of the revenue from Yemen oil industry, which is located in territory held by the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government of Yemen.Saudi Arabia is now being squeezed from three directions in the widening U.S.-Iran war — Iraq to its northeast, Yemen to its southwest, and Iran to its east. (On July 18, Tehran struck Prince Sultan Air Base near Riyadh, its first direct hit on Saudi soil in nearly four months.)To understand why this matters beyond the price of oil, it helps to picture the crises as a set of nesting dolls.The innermost doll is Yemen’s own civil war: a decade-old fight between the Houthis (officially known as Ansar Allah), who rule the populous north from Sana’a, and Yemen’s internationally recognized government, formally led by a body called the Presidential Leadership Council. The roots of this war trace to the 2011 Arab Spring revolution, which toppled Yemen’s long-serving president and left a power vacuum the Houthis moved to fill, seizing Sana’a in 2014. Saudi Arabia and a coalition of partners intervened in 2015 with the explicit aim of reversing that takeover and restoring the internationally recognized government, and the war has continued in one form or another ever since.The middle doll is Saudi Arabia’s broader rivalry with Iran, a contest for regional leadership that has run since Iran’s 1979 Islamic Revolution, when Tehran’s new theocratic government began exporting a revolutionary, Shia-inflected challenge to the Gulf’s Sunni monarchies.Since the Houthis’ seizure of Sana’a in September 2014, Iran has absorbed the group into what it calls its “axis of resistance,” supplying it with weapons, funding and technical know-how, turning Yemen into an arena of proxy war between Tehran and Riyadh.The outer doll is the American-Iranian war itself, now in its sixth month, which has all but closed the Strait of Hormuz and pushed oil prices to record highs. This conflict set the other two into motion.Since March 2022, an unofficial truce kept Yemen’s civil war, the Houthi-Saudi war, and the Saudi-Iranian rivalry in Yemen quiet even as the outer dolls rattled. That calm helped pave the way for a Saudi-Iranian rapprochement in 2023. What is new, and dangerous, is that all are now moving together.This month saw the fiercest clashes in years between Houthi fighters and government-aligned forces in the southern province of Dhale, which left dozens killed on both sides. Briefing reporters in Riyadh — where much of the official Yemeni government’s leadership operates — Yemen's new foreign minister, Afrah al-Zouba, said, “at the end of the day, we are prepared for any escalations.” She also warned that the “Houthis want to copy the Iran experience in Hormuz.”The trigger for current tensions was a July 3 Iranian Mahan Air flight, which landed in Houthi-held Sana’a to collect a delegation traveling to Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei’s funeral, the first such direct flight in more than a decade. Riyadh had long blocked exactly this kind of corridor, fearing it would be used to send weapons or military advisers to the Houthis.That fear proved well-founded, according to Reuters, which reported that the return flight on July 13th brought with it Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps personnel, along with missile and drone components. The Houthis have denied the accusations.Yemen’s internationally recognized government, backed by the Saudi-led coalition, has always treated the country’s airspace as remaining under its own legal authority. When that plane returned on July 13th, the government struck the airport runway to stop it landing again. The aircraft diverted to Hodeidah instead.That strike was not a unilateral decision. According to Axios, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman personally sought and received President Trump’s backing for the operation in a phone call days beforehand. Riyadh, it appeared, knew it was gambling with the Houthi truce and risked inflaming the already tense standoff between the U.S. and Iran, and wanted American cover before it moved.The Houthis retaliated within hours, firing missiles at Abha Airport in southern Saudi Arabia, the first direct strike on the kingdom in four years.All of this demonstrates how entangled Yemen’s civil war has become with the wider U.S.-Iran war. Iranian officials made this connection explicit while the Houthi delegation was in Tehran for Khamenei’s funeral.Ali Akbar Velayati, the supreme leader’s adviser, told the group that the siege of Yemen “must end immediately.” Parliament speaker, Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, praised Sana’a’s loyalty, stating that Ansar Allah “always stood by the resistance in defending Lebanon and Palestine.”Iran’s foreign ministry has stuck to a more measured public tone. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said there is “no military solution to the issue of Yemen,” and the ministry spokesman called for the U.N.-brokered 2023 roadmap to be “fully implemented.” However, this diplomatic call quietly endorses the Houthi narrative. Both officials characterized Sana’a as being under "siege," and under “continued blockade,” a clear acceptance of the Houthi framing of Saudi restrictions.Saudi Arabia, notably, has not pointed blame at Iran directly for inflaming tensions in Yemen. Instead, Yemeni officials have leveled these accusations. Yemen’s information minister, Moammar al-Iryani, stated outright that Houthi military decisions are now “more closely tied to directives from the Iranian Revolutionary Guard.”Riyadh has let its own client government make the accusations it avoids voicing directly, perhaps because naming Iran directly would foreclose the diplomatic space Riyadh still wants to maintain. That restraint would fit a broader pattern: Saudi Arabia has reportedly been keen to see the U.S.-Iran tensions resolved diplomatically rather than militarily, having already rejected Washington’s request to use Saudi airspace and bases for Project Freedom, the U.S. plan to escort ships through Hormuz.Riyadh, in other words, is hedging on multiple fronts at once. It is avoiding a total rupture with Tehran even as it fights Tehran’s allies on its southern flank and in Iraq, where it conducted airstrikes on Iran-aligned groups with the U.S. on July 28.That hedging leaves the door to de-escalation narrowed, but not fully shut. Oman, the traditional backchannel in Yemen’s civil war, said on July 23 that it was coordinating with Saudi Arabia, “Yemeni parties,” and the U.N.’s special envoy for Yemen to try to revive the stalled political process.That same weekend, Omani officials were in Tehran running a parallel negotiation on the Strait of Hormuz, shuttling between Iranian and American positions on ship-routing and transit fees.Oman is, in effect, trying to broker both of the region's thorniest disputes at once — a measure of how much regional diplomacy now runs through Muscat, and of how intertwined the conflicts have become.But diplomacy is losing ground. Reuters reported last week that Western officials involved in the Yemen mediation are increasingly pessimistic about reaching a negotiated resolution. Meanwhile, Houthi rhetoric towards its Yemeni rivals and Riyadh has grown increasingly fiery, and Saudi Arabia has made clear that attacks on its territory and tankers won't go unanswered.
